---
title: Thread MCP servers
description: "Giving a Pi Durable Platform agent your user's own MCP servers for one thread: when templates allow it, the allowed hosts, how headers are kept, proxy and direct modes, and tool names."
---

A chat app may let its users enable their own MCP servers, such as a personal notes server with the user's token. Your app can give those servers to an agent **for one thread**. The agent offers their tools in that thread only.

## When it's allowed

- The agent's template version must allow it: **Apps can give its agents their own MCP servers for a thread** (`clientMcp`).
- Each server's host must match `AGENTS_CLIENT_MCP_HOSTS`, which the operator sets. It's empty by default, which allows none.

Otherwise the request is refused (`client_mcp_not_allowed`, `client_mcp_host_not_allowed`).

## Give a thread its servers

With a message:

```json
{
  "text": "Add this to my notes",
  "requestId": "r9",
  "mcpServers": [
    {"name": "My notes", "url": "https://notes.example.com/mcp", "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer …"}, "expiresInSeconds": 3600}
  ]
}
```

or on their own:

```sh
PUT /v1/agents/{agentId}/threads/{threadId}/mcp-servers    # {servers: [{name, url, headers?, expiresInSeconds?}], visibility?}, replaces them
GET /v1/agents/{agentId}/threads/{threadId}/mcp-servers    # name, slug, url and expiry, never headers
```

- Up to 10 servers. Each `name` (up to 100 characters) is shown to the model and names the tools: `mcpc__<slug>__<tool>`.
- `headers` are encrypted and kept until the server expires: a day by default, at most a week (`expiresInSeconds`). They are never returned and never forwarded in the message.
- Sending a list replaces the thread's servers; `[]` removes them.
- The servers go with the thread: deleting the thread deletes them.

## Whose thread it is

A thread's servers always belong to a thread whose creator the platform knows. So giving servers to a thread ID that has no thread **starts the thread**, and you are its creator, exactly as sending its first message would. The `visibility` in the `PUT` body (`shared` by default, or `private`) is used only for this: send it before the first message when the thread is to be private. Starting a thread this way, like starting one with `POST /v1/agents/{agentId}/threads`, leaves it **reserved** until a message is accepted: only you see it in lists. A reserved thread that nobody sends to is removed after 30 days, with its servers.

When the thread already exists, you must be allowed on it:

| The thread | A request from you |
|---|---|
| Yours, or shared | Works. Anyone who may use the agent can read and change a shared thread's servers, and sees their names and URLs, never the headers |
| Someone else's, private | `404 thread_not_found`, as on every thread route |
| Any, with a `visibility` different from its own | `409 visibility_fixed` |

While a thread is reserved (nobody has sent to it yet), only its creator may set or clear its servers. Anyone else gets `404 thread_not_found`, so nobody can add servers that would be active for your first message without you knowing.

If someone else sends the first message to a shared thread you reserved with a client-chosen ID, the message goes through, but the servers you set are dropped: they are never active for their turn. The thread becomes an ordinary shared thread, and the sender's own `mcpServers` in that message apply.

An empty list for an ID with no thread changes nothing and starts nothing. A request with servers the platform refuses (a host that isn't allowed, or a template that doesn't allow them) starts nothing either.

Reading a thread's servers takes the same access as reading the thread.

## How the agent uses them

Before each message, the runtime fetches the thread's servers from the platform, lists their tools and offers them in that thread only. When the runtime restarts, it reinstalls every thread's servers, so a resumed reply keeps its tools.

`AGENTS_CLIENT_MCP_MODE` decides how the agent reaches them: through the platform's gateway (`proxy`, the default), which adds the headers, or `direct`, where the runtime gets the URL and headers.

## Things to know

- Servers are never kept for a thread that doesn't exist, so nobody can leave servers on an ID for someone else's later private thread to inherit. Whoever uses an ID later gets the rules of the thread they find. Start your threads with `POST /v1/agents/{agentId}/threads` (see [Start a thread](/docs/build/threads-and-messages#start-a-thread)): the ID can't be guessed, so no one else can start the thread first.
- These servers are separate from the MCP servers a template gives every thread of an agent ([Team MCP servers](/docs/teams/mcp-servers)).
